title: Is High Speed Internet the Reason You’re Not Married?
gist: A new working paper by economists Nathan Hudson and Hernan Moscoso Boedo uses the staggered rollout of 4G (starting December 2010) as a natural experiment and finds that faster local 4G adoption is linked to lower marriage rates among non-college-educated men, with the effect running through displaced socializing time (not lost work time) that then reduces marriageability and, eventually, work.

themes.theme: 4G rollout as a natural experiment on marriage

insights.claim: Economists Nathan Hudson and Hernan Moscoso Boedo (University of Cincinnati) use the staggered rollout of 4G mobile internet, which began in December 2010 and reached different U.S. commuting zones at different times, as a natural experiment to identify the effect of smartphone-era connectivity on marriage.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: A clean identification strategy (geographic/timing variation in tech rollout) for isolating technology's causal effect on family formation, generalizable to other tech-diffusion questions (broadband, social media, AI).
insights.quote: They focus on one development in particular: The rise of 4G mobile internet, which drastically improved web access on smartphones.

insights.claim: Using 4G deployment as of 2013 as the exposure measure and American Community Survey data to compare cohorts, the study finds an increasingly strong link between faster local 4G adoption and lower marriage rates among non-college-educated men — but not among college graduates.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: The marriage-suppressing effect of connectivity appears concentrated among non-college men, widening the marriage-market gap between college and non-college populations — relevant to labor-market and social-mobility forecasting.
insights.quote: there’s an increasingly strong link between how quickly an area adopted 4G and lower marriage rates for the non-college-educated men (but not college grads) who live there

insights.claim: Prior research using the iPhone's exclusivity deal with AT&T as a natural experiment found that births fell disproportionately within AT&T's smartphone coverage window relative to competing carriers, corroborating a causal link between early smartphone access and reduced family formation.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Two independent natural-experiment studies (fertility via AT&T/iPhone, marriage via 4G rollout) point the same direction, strengthening confidence that smartphone-era connectivity has a real, not just correlational, dampening effect on family formation.
insights.quote: other researchers used the iPhone’s exclusivity deal with AT&T to study smartphones’ effects on fertility ... finding that births fell disproportionately in AT&T’s coverage window, but not in those of competing services

themes.theme: Mechanism: screens displace socializing, not work

insights.claim: The paper's core mechanism is that increased male screen time in the smartphone era displaced time spent with friends and other leisure (like TV), not paid work directly; this reduced socializing lowered marriage rates, especially for men who were already less 'marriageable,' and only then did reduced marriage lower work, since married men historically work more than single men.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Identifies an indirect causal chain (screens → less socializing → less marriage → less work) rather than a direct one (screens → less work), which matters for designing interventions: fixing 'lazy men on screens' framing misses that the real leak is in social/dating time, not work hours.
insights.quote: The increase in men’s screen time during the smartphone era hasn’t come directly at the expense of work. Instead, it mostly displaced time with friends and other forms of leisure.

insights.claim: Analysis of the American Time Use Survey shows that extra screen time among single men came mostly out of TV-watching and time with friends, not out of work time; solitary screen leisure increased far less among women and married men.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Confirms the displacement is concentrated in single men's social time specifically, supporting targeted interventions (e.g., in-person social infrastructure) over blanket 'get off your phone and get a job' framing.
insights.quote: the extra time that single men are spending alone with their screens is not taking them away from work ... it's taking them away from other forms of leisure like TV, as well as time with friends
insights.locator: paragraph on American Time Use Survey analysis

insights.claim: Since married men have historically worked more than single men, a decline in marriage rates mechanically explains part of the drop in male labor-force participation.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Reframes some of the 'men dropping out of the workforce' narrative as downstream of the marriage decline itself, rather than a purely independent labor-supply or motivation problem.
insights.quote: since married men have always worked more than single men, reducing marriage rates eventually reduces men’s work, too

themes.theme: Scale of the marriage and labor-force decline

insights.claim: Among non-college-educated men ages 21-30, the marriage rate fell from about 32% in the mid-2000s to 21% in the late 2010s, and this shift into the unmarried category (where non-work is more common) statistically explains around a third of the drop in labor-force participation for that group over the same period.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Quantifies the marriage-to-labor-supply linkage at roughly one-third of the observed decline — a specific, testable magnitude for economists and policymakers modeling male labor-force attachment.
insights.quote: about 32% of non-college-educated men ages 21 to 30 were married, which fell to 21% in the late 2010s. By itself, more men remaining in the unmarried category ... statistically explains around a third of the drop in labor-force participation
insights.locator: paragraph with mid-2000s to late-2010s marriage-rate figures

insights.claim: The decline in marriage has the opposite labor-supply effect for women, who tend to work less for pay after marrying and having kids, effectively 'redistributing labor supply across the genders' as marriage rates fall.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: The marriage decline is not labor-supply-neutral: it likely pushes male labor supply down and female labor supply up simultaneously, a structural factor relevant to workforce composition forecasts.
insights.quote: the decline of marriage thus “redistribute[es] labor supply across the genders.”
insights.locator: paragraph on gender asymmetry in the marriage/work link

insights.claim: IFS survey data cited in the piece found that nearly a quarter of young men gamble daily, more than two in five watch pornography daily, and about the same share play video games daily.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of daily habitual screen/vice consumption among young men, a relevant baseline for assessing exposure to online gambling and content platforms as behavioral/social-cost drivers, not just entertainment categories.
insights.quote: nearly a quarter of young men are now gambling daily, more than two in five watch porn every day, and about the same share play video games daily
insights.locator: paragraph on broader technology and disconnection trend

insights.claim: The author frames the findings cautiously: this is a working paper with many caveats, studying a tangle of issues where causation can run in multiple directions, and its authors present it as suggestive rather than definitive evidence.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Appropriate epistemic caution: treat the 4G-marriage link as one contributing factor among many long-running trends (marriage and work decline predate smartphones), not a mono-causal explanation.
insights.quote: This is a working paper with a lot of caveats, studying a tangle of issues where causation can run in a lot of different directions at once. So we should not take its findings as gospel.

insights.claim: The author's thesis is that unmarriageable men ('duds') are disproportionately absorbed into solitary screen habits that further reduce their odds of marrying, compounding an existing selection effect rather than creating an entirely new one.
insights.speaker: Robert VerBruggen
insights.so_what: Implies that policy or product interventions aimed at reducing screen time alone may have limited effect on marriage rates unless they also address the underlying marriageability/social-skill gap among affected men.
insights.quote: guys don’t quit their jobs to play Fortnite and stare at their phones, but these habits do hold up their relationships, especially if they weren’t great catches to begin with
insights.locator: paragraph after discussion of Time Use Survey
